£40,000 Salary After Tax UK

On a £40,000 salary in England, Wales or Northern Ireland you take home £32,320 a year in 2026/27: £2,693 a month, £622 a week or £16.57 an hour on a 37.5-hour week. You pay £5,486 Income Tax and £2,194 National Insurance, so you keep 80.8% of your gross pay.

What £40,000 means for your take-home pay

Just over £10,000 below higher rate

You need a further £10,270 of pay before the 40% rate starts at £50,270. Until then each extra pound keeps 72p (28% deducted).

Plan 2 costs about £80 a month

A Plan 2 loan takes £955 a year (£80 a month) on £40,000, because you repay 9% of the £10,615 above the £29,385 threshold. That leaves £2,614 a month.

A cushion for pension top-ups

Paying 8% into a pension via salary sacrifice (£3,200 a year) reduces take-home by £2,304. You are unlikely to reach the higher-rate band, so relief is at 20% plus 8% NI.

What would a pay change do to your take-home?

Compare your salary above with a raise, promotion or job offer. Higher-rate tax, National Insurance and student loan all change how much you keep.

+£10,000 gross+£600 / month net

Moving from £40,000 to £50,000 changes your take-home by +£7,200 a year (+£600 a month). You keep 72% of the extra gross pay; the rest goes in Income Tax and National Insurance. Your next pound at the new salary is taxed at a combined 28%.

Frequently asked questions

How much is £40,000 a year after tax in the UK?

In 2026/27, £40,000 leaves £32,320 a year after £5,486 Income Tax and £2,194 National Insurance in England, Wales and Northern Ireland. That is £2,693 a month.

How much is £40,000 a month after tax?

About £2,693 a month, or £622 a week, assuming tax code 1257L and no pension or student loan.

What is the hourly rate for £40,000?

Before tax, £40,000 is £20.51 an hour on a 37.5-hour week (£19.23 on 40 hours). After tax it is £16.57 an hour.

What tax band is £40,000 in?

The basic-rate band. You pay 20% on pay over £12,570, and your marginal rate including 8% NI is 28%.

How much less would I take home in Scotland on £40,000?

About £65 a year less, because Scottish Income Tax is £65 higher on this salary in 2026/27.

Does a student loan change £40,000 after tax?

Yes. A Plan 2 loan would take £955 a year on this salary, leaving £31,364. Use the calculator above to try your own plan.
